query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated approach that couples ab initio thermodynamic integration with machine learning models can accurately and efficiently determine the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys over a broad compositional space.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid-phase high-entropy alloys characterized by multi-element disordered crystalline structures.
generation.intervention: Application of ab initio thermodynamic integration to obtain free energy differences during melting, with machine learning used to interpolate and predict properties across different alloy compositions.
generation.conditions: Ambient pressure with temperature ramping through the melting regime under controlled isothermal/isobaric conditions to simulate and measure phase transitions.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical disorder and atomic-scale interactions within the high-entropy alloy microstructure that influence melting behavior.
generation.mechanism: The method relies on first-principles calculations to compute accurate interatomic potentials and free energy landscapes near the melting point, while machine learning accelerates the exploration of compositional space by interpolating between computed data points. This dual strategy is expected to capture both local atomic interactions and global thermodynamic trends.
generation.predicted_outcome: Predicted values of melting temperature, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and associated liquid-phase properties that lie within a ±5-10% error margin compared to high-precision experimental measurements.
generation.baseline: Existing methods which either rely solely on experimental techniques or on computational approaches that are computationally intensive and limited in compositional applicability.
generation.boundary: The approach might fail in alloy compositions exhibiting extreme local ordering effects or chemical clustering not well represented in the training data, and may be less predictive under non-ambient pressure conditions or outside the calibrated temperature range.
generation.uncertainty: There is no direct prior evidence provided in the eligible records to support the feasibility or accuracy of combining ab initio thermodynamic integration with machine learning in this context. The performance and applicability of the method across the entire high-entropy alloy family remain uncertain until validated by comprehensive experiments.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a diverse set of high-entropy alloys covering a broad compositional range. Carry out high-precision calorimetric and structural measurements during phase transitions and compare these with predictions generated by the integrated approach under identical conditions.
measurements: Melting temperature using differential scanning calorimetry
Enthalpy and entropy of fusion through high-resolution calorimetry techniques
Volume change at melting via in situ X-ray diffraction or dilatometry
Liquid-phase properties using high-temperature viscosity and density measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predictions from the integrated computational approach deviate by more than 10% from the experimental measurements over the majority of alloy compositions tested, the hypothesis is falsified.

decision.trend: Early studies in HEAs have largely focused on two approaches. One strand (exemplified by PMC8282813) has employed high‐throughput computational screening to identify alloys with desired high-temperature strength and melting‐temperature thresholds, thus indirectly inferring thermodynamic performance. Another strand (e.g., PMC9229239) has pushed rapid synthesis techniques (like LPBF) that yield fine microstructures and accelerate processing, albeit without directly resolving the detailed thermodynamics at melting. Overall, the field has progressed from traditional DSC and static calorimetric techniques—which lack sensitivity and throughput for the vast compositional space—to high-throughput and rapid-processing experiments. However, none of these studies has yet delivered a method that can directly and efficiently measure the fusion enthalpy, entropy, and the associated volume change along with liquid-phase properties across all HEAs.
decision.unsolved: An efficient method capable of simultaneously delivering high-accuracy measurements of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamics -- with a clearly founded physical rationale and quantitative performance benchmarks -- has not been achieved. Existing experimental techniques either lack the sensitivity and speed required or are restricted by compositional limitations, while computational models struggle with the intrinsic complexity of multi-principal-element systems.
decision.lever: integrated fast-scanning calorimetry combined with in situ high-speed synchrotron X-ray diffraction
decision.why: This approach builds on the trend toward high-throughput and rapid synthesis while directly targeting the accurate detection of rapid thermodynamic changes at the solid-liquid transition. The fast-scanning calorimetry offers high temporal resolution and sensitivity to capture enthalpy/entropy changes, and the in situ diffraction provides decisive structural validation (e.g., detecting abrupt volume changes). Such integration directly addresses the need for both accuracy and efficiency across a wide range of HEA compositions, fitting the cues and limitations highlighted in prior work.
